CH3CHCH2CH=CH2 with the carbons numbered 5,4,3,2,1 from right to left so the double bond gets the lowest numbers, and a CH3 branch on carbon 4 labeled 'Methyl group'.
CH3CH=CHCHCH3 with a CH3 group below the fourth carbon (4-methyl-2-pentene).
CH3CH=CCH2CH3 with a CH3 group below the third carbon (3-methyl-2-pentene).
CH3CH2CHCH=CHCH2CH3 with a CH3 group below the third carbon from the left.
A five-carbon chain C-C=C-C-C numbered 1 to 5 in red, with the double bond between carbons 2 and 3.
CH3CH=CCH2CH3 with a CH3 group below carbon 3: 3-methyl-2-pentene with all hydrogens added.
Line-angle structure of cyclohexene: a hexagon with one double bond drawn on one edge.

(b) 1,2-dichloroethene: a double spring prevents rotation, so the trans and cis arrangements are different molecules, isomers.

Ball-and-spring models of (a) cis-2-butene, with both CH3 groups on the same side of the double bond, and (b) trans-2-butene, with the CH3 groups on opposite sides.
Structural formulas of cis-2-butene (both CH3 groups above the C=C, both H below) and trans-2-butene (one CH3 above and one below), each labeled.
Two drawings of propene that look different (the CH3 on the left carbon pointing up, or pointing down) but are the same molecule, because the left carbon carries two identical H atoms.
Cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (both CH3 groups above the ring, drawn with wedges) and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (one CH3 above and one below the ring), each labeled.
Two isomers of 1-bromo-2-chloroethene: Cl (green) and Br (orange) on the same side of the C=C, and Cl and Br on opposite sides.

CH3C=CHCH3 with a CH3 group below the second carbon (2-methyl-2-butene): the second carbon carries two identical CH3 groups, so no cis-trans isomers exist.
597080: Photograph of four ripe red tomatoes on the vine.
Line-angle structure of lycopene: a very long chain of alternating single and double bonds (a conjugated polyene) with methyl branches along its length and branched ends.

A segment of polyvinyl chloride: a chain of alternating CH2 and CH units, each CH bearing a Cl atom, with tildes at each end showing the chain continues.
Two drawings of a hip joint: a natural ball-and-socket joint, and the same joint replaced with a metal ball and stem fitted into a polymer socket.
597083: Ball-and-spring model of acetylene: two red carbon spheres joined by three springs (a triple bond) in a straight line, each with one light-blue hydrogen.

Three benzene derivatives with common names: toluene (ring with CH3), phenol (ring with OH) and aniline (ring with NH2).

The three dichlorobenzenes: 1,2-dichlorobenzene (o-dichlorobenzene) with Cl atoms on adjacent carbons, 1,3-dichlorobenzene (m-) with Cl atoms separated by one carbon, and 1,4-dichlorobenzene (p-) with Cl atoms on opposite carbons.

Four disubstituted benzenes with both IUPAC and common names: 1-bromo-4-chlorobenzene (p-bromochlorobenzene), 2-bromophenol (o-bromophenol, OH and Br adjacent), 3-chloroaniline (m-chloroaniline, NH2 and Cl separated by one carbon) and 3-bromotoluene (m-bromotoluene, CH3 and Br meta).
A benzene ring with two Cl atoms on adjacent carbons.
A benzene ring with a CH3 group and a Br atom on opposite carbons.
A benzene ring with two NO2 groups separated by one carbon (meta).
2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT): a benzene ring with a CH3 group at the top and NO2 groups on the two carbons beside it and on the carbon opposite.
A benzene ring with two Br atoms on adjacent carbons.
A benzene ring with an NH2 group and a Br atom on adjacent carbons.
A benzene ring with a Br at the top and a Cl on each neighboring carbon.

The phenyl group written as C6H5 with an open bond, 'or' as a benzene ring with an open bond, labeled 'Phenyl group'; beside it 2-phenylheptane, CH3CHCH2CH2CH2CH2CH3 with a C6H5 group below the second carbon.
Three polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons: naphthalene (two fused benzene rings), anthracene (three rings fused in a row) and phenanthrene (three rings fused at an angle), each labeled.
Structure of aspirin: a benzene ring with a COOH group and, on the adjacent carbon, an OCOCH3 (acetyl ester) group.
Structure of acetaminophen: a benzene ring with an HO group and, on the opposite carbon, an NHCOCH3 amide group.
Structure of ibuprofen as drawn: a benzene ring with a four-carbon branched alkyl group (a CH bearing CH3 and CH2CH3) on one carbon and a CH(CH3)COOH group on the opposite carbon.
Structure of amphetamine: a benzene ring attached to a CH2CH(CH3) chain that carries an NH2 group.
Structure of sulfanilamide: a benzene ring with an NH2 group and, on the opposite carbon, an SO2NH2 group.
597090: The alkene functional group: C=C with two open bonds on each carbon.
General formula of an aldehyde: R-CH=O, a carbon double-bonded to O and bonded to an R group and an H.
The aldehyde functional group: a carbon with a double bond to O, a bond to H, and one open bond.
General formula of a ketone: R-C(=O)-R, a carbon double-bonded to O and bonded to two R groups.
The ketone functional group: a carbon with a double bond to O and two open bonds.
General formula of a carboxylic acid: R-C(=O)-OH, a carbon double-bonded to O and bonded to an OH group and an R group.
The carboxylic acid functional group: a carbon with a double bond to O, a bond to OH, and one open bond.
597091: Condensed formulas with common names: CH3OH methyl alcohol, CH3CH2OH ethyl alcohol, CH3CH2CH2OH propyl alcohol, and CH3CHOH with a CH3 below (isopropyl alcohol).
A ten-carbon chain CH3CH2CHCH2CHCH2CH2CHCH2CH3 with CH3 groups below the third and fifth carbons from the left and an OH below the eighth carbon.
The same ten-carbon chain numbered 10 down to 1 from left to right in red, so the OH is on carbon 3 and the methyl groups are on carbons 6 and 8: 6,8-dimethyl-3-decanol.
HOCH2CH2CH2CH2CH2OH with the five carbons numbered 1 to 5: 1,5-pentanediol.
CH3CHCH2OH with an OH below the second carbon: 1,2-propanediol.
A cyclopentane ring (pentagon) with an OH and a CH3 group on the same carbon: 1-methylcyclopentanol.
A six-carbon skeleton C-C-C-C-C-C with an OH drawn below the second carbon: the parent chain for 2-hexanol before hydrogens are added.
CH3CHCH2CH2CH2CH3 with an OH below the second carbon: 2-hexanol with all hydrogens added.
CH3CH-CHCH2CH3 with OH below the second carbon and CH3 below the third carbon: 3-methyl-2-pentanol.
A primary alcohol: a central carbon (red) bonded to OH, two H atoms and one R group (blue).
A secondary alcohol: a central carbon (red) bonded to OH, one H and two R groups (blue).
A tertiary alcohol: a central carbon (red) bonded to OH and three R groups (blue).
Three butyl groups: isobutyl (CH3CHCH2- with a CH3 branch), sec-butyl (CH3CHCH2CH3 attached at the CH) and tert-butyl (a carbon bonded to three CH3 groups), each labeled.
A cyclohexane ring drawn in green with an OH group attached: cyclohexanol.
597092: Water drawn as H-O-H (one H in red) beside an alcohol drawn as R-O-H, showing that an alcohol is water with one H replaced by an R group.

Ball-and-stick drawing of four methanol molecules; green dotted lines between the O-H hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another mark hydrogen bonds. A key reads 'green dots = hydrogen bonding'.
Ball-and-stick drawing of an ethanol molecule hydrogen-bonded (green dotted lines) to several water molecules, labeled 'Water' and 'Ethanol'; a key reads 'green dots = hydrogen bonding'.
597093: Hydration of ethylene: H2C=CH2 plus H2O (blue), with H plus over the arrow, gives ethanol, drawn with the added H on one carbon and OH (blue) on the other.
Propylene (CH2=CHCH3) plus H-OH (blue), with H2SO4 over the arrow, gives isopropyl alcohol (2-propanol), CH3CHCH3 with OH (blue) on the middle carbon.
CH3CH=CHCH3 plus H2O (blue), with H2SO4 over the arrow, gives CH3CHCH2CH3 with OH (blue) below the second carbon (2-butanol).
Fumarate, minus OOCCH=CHCOO minus, plus HOH (blue), with 'enzyme' over a double arrow, gives malate, minus OOCCH2CHOHCOO minus, with the added OH in blue.
Fermentation: starch, (C6H10O5)n, with 'enzymes' over the arrow, gives glucose, C6H12O6, which with 'enzymes' over a second arrow gives 2 CH3CH2OH (ethanol) plus 2 CO2.
Methanol, CH3OH, with 'liver enzymes' over the arrow, gives formaldehyde, H-C(=O)-H.
Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, with 'liver enzymes' over the arrow, gives acetaldehyde, CH3-CH=O.
597094: Flowchart of alcohol reactions. From 'an alcohol' three branches lead to oxidation (K2Cr2O7, acid): a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde, which oxidizes further to a carboxylic acid; a secondary alcohol gives a ketone; a tertiary alcohol gives no reaction. A dehydration branch (concentrated H2SO4, heat) gives an alkene (excess acid, 180 degrees C) or an ether (excess alcohol, 140 degrees C). An esterification branch (carboxylic acid, acid catalyst) gives an ester.

Dehydration of ethanol: the expanded formula of ethanol, with the H on one carbon and the OH on the other shown in blue, with 'concd H2SO4, 180 degrees C, excess acid' over the arrow, gives ethylene (H2C=CH2) plus HOH (blue).
Two molecules of ethanol, CH3CH2OH plus HOCH2CH3 (the OH groups in green), with 'concd H2SO4, 140 degrees C, excess ethanol' over the arrow, give diethyl ether, CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3, plus H2O (green).

2-Phosphoglycerate, drawn with a blue OH and a blue H on adjacent carbons plus COO minus and OPO3 2 minus groups, with 'enzyme' over the arrow, gives phosphoenolpyruvate (a C=C bearing COO minus and OPO3 2 minus) plus HOH (blue).
Ethanol, CH3CH2OH (a primary alcohol), with [O] over the arrow, gives acetaldehyde, CH3CH=O (an aldehyde); the atoms that change are shown in green.
Isopropyl alcohol, CH3CHCH3 with a blue OH (a secondary alcohol), with 'K2Cr2O7, H plus' over the arrow, gives acetone, CH3-C(=O)-CH3 with the O in blue (a ketone).
Isocitrate, a three-carbon chain bearing three COOH groups with an HO (blue) on the end carbon, with 'enzyme' over the arrow, gives oxalosuccinate, in which that carbon is now a C=O (blue).
CH3CCH2CH3 with a CH3 above and an OH below the second carbon: 2-methyl-2-butanol, a tertiary alcohol.
CH3CHCH2CH2CH2CH3 with an OH below the second carbon: 2-hexanol, a secondary alcohol.
CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH (1-pentanol), with [O] over the arrow, gives the aldehyde CH3CH2CH2CH2CH=O; a second [O] arrow gives the carboxylic acid CH3CH2CH2CH2COOH.
CH3CCH2CH3 with CH3 above and OH below the second carbon (a tertiary alcohol), with [O] over the arrow, gives 'no reaction'.
CH3CHCH2CH2CH2CH3 with OH on the second carbon (2-hexanol), with [O] over the arrow, gives CH3C(=O)CH2CH2CH2CH3 (2-hexanone).
CH3CH2CCH2CH2CH3 with an OH above and a CH3 below the third carbon: 3-methyl-3-hexanol, a tertiary alcohol.
CH3CHCH2OH with a CH3 below the second carbon: 2-methyl-1-propanol, a primary alcohol.
CH3CHCHCH2CH2CH3 with an OH above the second carbon and a CH3 below the third carbon: 3-methyl-2-hexanol, a secondary alcohol.
597095: CH3CHCH2OH with an OH below the second carbon, labeled 'Propylene glycol'.
HOCH2CHCH2OH with an OH below the middle carbon, labeled 'Glycerol'.
Ethylene glycol, HOCH2CH2OH, with [O] over the arrow, gives the oxalate ion, two C=O carbons bonded together, each bearing an O minus.
Propylene glycol, CH3CHCH2OH with OH on the middle carbon, with [O] over the arrow, gives the pyruvate ion, CH3-C(=O)-C(=O)-O minus.
597096: Ball-and-stick model of phenol: a six-carbon aromatic ring (dark gray spheres) with an OH group (red oxygen, white hydrogen) attached to one carbon.
Photograph of colorless phenol crystals in a glass test tube.
Oil painting of an eighteenth-century surgical operation: a patient is held down by assistants while a surgeon works, before the age of anesthesia or antiseptics.
Structure of 4-hexylresorcinol: a benzene ring with two OH groups on adjacent carbons and a six-carbon hexyl chain (CH2CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3) on the carbon opposite one of them.
597097: CH3CHOCH3 with a CH3 below the CH: isopropyl methyl ether, an oxygen bonded to an isopropyl group and a methyl group.
A cyclobutane ring (square) bonded to an OCH2CH3 group: cyclobutyl ethyl ether.
Painting of the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia (1846): a dentist leans over a patient reclining in a chair, holding an inhaler to the patient's face while onlookers watch.
Structures of three inhaled anesthetics with the halogens colored: halothane (H-CBr(Cl)-CF3), enflurane (HCF2-O-CF2-CHClF) and isoflurane (HCF2-O-CHCl-CF3), each labeled.
597102: The carbonyl group: a carbon with a double bond to O and two open bonds.
Three general ketone formulas: R-C(=O)-R, Ar-C(=O)-R and Ar-C(=O)-Ar, where Ar is an aromatic ring; the carbonyl O is in green.
Three general aldehyde formulas: H-C(=O)-H (formaldehyde), R-C(=O)-H and Ar-C(=O)-H; the carbonyl O and the aldehyde H are in green.
Condensed notations: -CHO (in green) labeled 'An aldehyde' and -CO- (in green) labeled 'A ketone'.
Two oxidations: formaldehyde, H-CH=O, with [O] over the arrow, gives formic acid, H-C(=O)-OH; acetaldehyde, CH3-CH=O, with [O], gives acetic acid, CH3-C(=O)-OH. The added OH is in green.
CH3-C(=O)-CH3 with the carbonyl in green, labeled 'Acetone'.
CH3-C(=O)-CH2CH3, labeled 'Ethyl methyl ketone'.
CH3CH2CH2-C(=O)-H: butanal, an aldehyde with a three-carbon chain on the carbonyl carbon.
CH3CH2CH2-C(=O)-CH2CH2CH3: 4-heptanone, a carbonyl carbon bonded to two propyl groups.
CH3-C(=O)-CHCH3 with a CH3 above the CH: 3-methyl-2-butanone, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl and an isopropyl group.
CH3CH2CH2-C(=O)-CH2CH3: 3-hexanone.
CH3CH2CH-C(=O)-H with a CH3 above the CH: 2-methylbutanal.
A cyclobutane ring (square) bonded to C(=O)-CH3: cyclobutyl methyl ketone.
CH3CH2CH2CH-C(=O)-H with a CH3 above the CH: 2-methylpentanal.
CH3CH-C(=O)-CHCH3 with a CH3 above each CH: 2,4-dimethyl-3-pentanone.
A hexagon with a C=O on one corner: cyclohexanone.
CH3CCH2-C(=O)-H with CH3 groups above and below the second carbon: 3,3-dimethylbutanal.
CH3CH-C(=O)-CH2CH2CH3 with a CH3 above the CH: 2-methyl-3-hexanone.
A square ring with a C=O on one corner: cyclobutanone.
CH3CHCH2CH2CH2CH2CH2CHO with a Cl below the second carbon from the left: 7-chlorooctanal.
CH3CH2-C(=O)-CHCH2CH3 with a CH3 above the CH: 4-methyl-3-hexanone.
597103: A carbonyl group with two R groups on the carbon; the carbon is marked delta plus (partial positive) and the oxygen delta minus (partial negative).
A carbonyl compound R2C=O hydrogen-bonded (dotted line) from its oxygen to the H of a water molecule, H-O-H.
An aldehyde, R-CH=O, with [O] over the arrow, gives a carboxylic acid, R-C(=O)-OH; a ketone, R-C(=O)-R, with [O], gives 'no reaction'. The carbonyl groups are in green.
Photograph of a worker in green gloves lifting a rack of freshly silvered glass items from a tank, illustrating the silver-mirror process.

Five aldehydes: (a) benzaldehyde, a benzene ring with a CHO group; (b) cinnamaldehyde, a benzene ring attached to CH=CH-CHO; (c) vanillin, a benzene ring bearing CHO, OH and OCH3 groups; (d) a C=C double bond with CH3CH2 on one carbon and CH2CHO on the other, both H on the same side (cis-3-hexenal); (e) a chain with two C=C double bonds, CH3CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH=CH-CHO (2,6-nonadienal).

Four ketones: (a) 2,3-butanedione, CH3-C(=O)-C(=O)-CH3; (b) beta-ionone, a cyclohexene ring with methyl groups attached to a CH=CH-C(=O)-CH3 side chain; (c) muscone, a large fifteen-membered ring containing a C=O and a methyl branch; (d) camphor, a bicyclic structure with a C=O and three methyl groups.
597104: Mechanism of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl. Step 1: a nucleophile (Nu minus) attacks the carbonyl carbon of the substrate R-C(=O)-R prime (red arrows show the electron movement), giving a tetrahedral intermediate with O minus and Nu on the same carbon. Step 2: the O minus takes a proton from H-B plus to give the product, with OH and Nu on that carbon.

Cyanohydrin formation: cyanide (N triple-bond C minus) attacks acetone in step 1 to give a tetrahedral intermediate with O minus, then step 2 protonation by H-B plus gives a cyanohydrin, a carbon bearing OH, C triple-bond N and two CH3 groups.

Cyanohydrin formation from ethanal: cyanide attacks the aldehyde carbon in step 1 to give a tetrahedral intermediate with O minus, then step 2 protonation by H-B plus gives a cyanohydrin bearing OH, C triple-bond N, CH3 and H on one carbon.

Seven-step mechanism in which a nucleophile H-Nu adds twice to a carbonyl. Top row: the substrate is protonated, the first nucleophilic addition gives tetrahedral intermediate I, proton transfers give intermediates II and III. Bottom row: loss of water gives a C=Nu plus cation, a second nucleophilic addition gives intermediate IV, and deprotonation gives the product with two Nu groups on the carbon. Red curved arrows show electron movement.
An aldehyde or a ketone, R-C(=O)-R prime, plus H2O, with H3O plus over a double arrow, gives a hydrate: a carbon bearing two OH groups, R and R prime.
Acetone plus H2O, with H3O plus over a double arrow, gives the hydrate H3C-C(OH)2-CH3, labeled 0.2 percent.
Formaldehyde, H2C=O, plus H2O, with H3O plus over a double arrow, gives the hydrate H-C(OH)2-H, labeled 99.9 percent.
Acetaldehyde, CH3CH=O, plus H2O, with H3O plus over a double arrow, gives the hydrate H3C-C(OH)2-H, labeled 58 percent.
Acetone plus HO-CH3 (limited supply), with H3O plus over a double arrow, gives a hemiacetal: a carbon bearing OH, OCH3 and two CH3 groups.
Open-chain Fischer-style drawing of glucose: a six-carbon chain with a CHO group at the top right, HOCH2 at the bottom left, and H and OH groups on each of the four middle carbons.
Acetone plus HO-CH3 (excess), with H3O plus over a double arrow, gives an acetal, a carbon bearing two OCH3 groups and two CH3 groups, plus water.

Ring structures of three disaccharides with the acetal linkage between the two sugar rings circled in yellow: lactose (glucose plus galactose), maltose (glucose plus glucose) and sucrose (glucose plus fructose).
597105: Oxidation states of carbon in one-carbon compounds, shown in red. Top row, under a gray arrow labeled 'Oxidation' pointing right: methane (minus 4), methanol (minus 2), methanal (0), methanoic acid (plus 2), carbon dioxide (plus 4). Bottom row, under a gray arrow labeled 'Reduction' pointing left: the two-carbon compounds ethane, ethanol, ethanal and ethanoic acid with the oxidation state of each carbon.
Ethene, H2C=CH2, plus H-H, with an arrow, gives 'No reaction'.
Ethene, H2C=CH2, plus H-H (red), with Ni over the arrow, gives ethane with the two added H atoms shown in red.

Mechanism of catalytic hydrogenation drawn in four panels: H2 and the alkene adsorb onto the catalyst surface, the H-H bond breaks into surface H atoms, the H atoms add one at a time to the same face of the C=C, and the alkane leaves the surface.

Partial hydrogenation of a vegetable oil. Top: a triglyceride (glycerol backbone with three ester-linked chains) with two linoleic chains (two cis C=C each) and one oleic chain (one cis C=C). An arrow labeled H2, Ni leads to the bottom triglyceride with one stearic chain (fully saturated) and two oleic chains.
Butanal, CH3CH2CH2CH=O, plus H-H, with Ni over the arrow, gives 1-butanol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH.
Cyclohexanone (a hexagon with C=O) plus H-H, with Ni over the arrow, gives cyclohexanol (a hexagon with OH).
2-Butenal, CH3CH=CHCH=O, plus 2 H-H, with Ni over the arrow, gives 1-butanol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH; both the C=C and the C=O are reduced.

Simplified mechanism of NaBH4 reduction: a hydride (H minus, red) from Na plus BH4 minus attacks the carbonyl carbon of R-C(=O)-R prime (step 1), giving an alkoxide intermediate coordinated to BH3Na plus; protonation by H-B plus (step 2) gives the alcohol with the new H in red.
2-Butenal, CH3CH=CHCH=O, with '1. NaBH4, 2. H3O plus' over the arrow, gives 2-buten-1-ol, CH3CH=CHCH2OH; the C=O is reduced but the C=C is not.

Structures of NAD plus (left) and NADH (right): a nicotinamide ring (highlighted in yellow) attached through a ribose and two phosphates to an adenosine; in NADH the nicotinamide ring has an extra hydrogen and no positive charge.
Acetaldehyde, CH3CH=O, plus NADH plus H plus, with 'alcohol dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives ethanol, CH3CH2OH, plus NAD plus.
Pyruvate, CH3-C(=O)-COO minus, plus NADH plus H plus, with 'lactate dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives lactate, CH3-CH(OH)-COO minus, plus NAD plus.

Simplified mechanism of LiAlH4 reduction of an acid chloride: hydride adds to the carbonyl, chloride leaves to give an aldehyde, a second hydride adds, and protonation gives the primary alcohol; red curved arrows show the electron movement.
Propanoyl chloride, CH3CH2-C(=O)-Cl, with '1. 2 NaBH4, 2. H3O plus' over the arrow, gives 1-propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH.
Propanoyl chloride, CH3CH2-C(=O)-Cl, with '1. LiAlH4, 2. H3O plus' over the arrow, gives 1-propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH.
Propanoic acid, CH3CH2-C(=O)-OH, with '1. LiAlH4, 2. H3O plus' over the arrow, gives 1-propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH.
Methyl propanoate, CH3CH2-C(=O)-OCH3, with '1. LiAlH4, 2. H3O plus' over the arrow, gives 1-propanol, CH3CH2CH2OH, plus methanol, CH3OH.
N-methylpropanamide, CH3CH2-C(=O)-NHCH3, with '1. LiAlH4, 2. H3O plus' over the arrow, gives the amine CH3CH2CH2-NHCH3.

Mechanism of alcohol oxidation by chromic acid (Jones reagent): the alcohol oxygen attacks chromium to form a chromate ester, then a base removes the carbon's H while the C=O forms and the chromium species leaves; red curved arrows show the electron movement.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid: ethanol, with 'CrO3 plus H2SO4' over the arrow, gives ethanal; ethanal plus H2O gives (double arrow) the hydrate with two OH groups; the hydrate, with 'CrO3 plus H2SO4', gives ethanoic acid.
2-Propanol, CH3CH(OH)CH3, with 'CrO3 plus H2SO4' over the arrow, gives acetone, CH3C(=O)CH3.
Photograph of two test tubes in a beaker: the left tube is coated inside with a shiny silver mirror (positive Tollens test for an aldehyde) and the right tube is clear (negative test).

Eight test tubes labeled 'Benedict's test for sugars' showing the color of the result with increasing sugar concentration: blue (0 percent), green, yellow-green, yellow, orange, red-orange, red and brown (greater than 4 percent).
Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, plus NAD plus, with 'alcohol dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives ethanal, CH3CH=O, plus NADH plus H plus.
Methanol, CH3OH, plus NAD plus, with 'alcohol dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives methanal, H2C=O, plus NADH plus H plus.
Lactate, CH3CH(OH)COO minus, plus NAD plus, with 'lactate dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives pyruvate, CH3C(=O)COO minus, plus NADH plus H plus.
597106: Flowchart classifying isomers. Expanded skeletal drawing of hexane: a six-carbon zigzag chain written as H3C-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3.

Expanded skeletal drawing of 3-methylpentane: a five-carbon chain with a CH3 group on the middle carbon.
Expanded skeletal drawing of 2,3-dimethylbutane: two CH carbons bonded together, each bearing two CH3 groups.
Expanded skeletal drawing of 2,2-dimethylbutane: a carbon bearing three CH3 groups bonded to a CH2CH3 group.
Expanded skeletal drawing of propan-1-ol: H3C-CH2-CH2-OH.

Expanded skeletal drawing of propan-1-ol: H3C-CH2-CH2-OH, with the OH on an end carbon.
Expanded skeletal drawing of propan-2-ol: a central C bearing OH and H, bonded to two CH3 groups; a positional isomer of propan-1-ol.

Two conformations of ethane drawn in three dimensions: the eclipsed form, with a 60-degree label showing the rotation needed, and the staggered form, in which the H atoms on the two carbons are offset.
Ball-and-stick model of ethane in a staggered conformation.
Anti conformer of butane drawn in three dimensions: the two CH3 groups on adjacent carbons point in opposite directions.
Gauche conformer of butane drawn in three dimensions: the two CH3 groups on adjacent carbons are close together, 60 degrees apart.
cis-But-2-ene: H3C-CH=CH-CH3 with both CH3 groups on the same side of the double bond.
trans-But-2-ene: H3C-CH=CH-CH3 with the CH3 groups on opposite sides of the double bond.
A chiral carbon drawn with wedge-and-dash bonds: CHO above, H to the left, CH3 on a dashed bond to the right, and OH on a wedge below (the page labels this D-glyceraldehyde).
The mirror image of the previous structure: CHO above, H to the right, CH3 on a dashed bond to the left, and OH on a wedge below (labeled L-glyceraldehyde).

Illustration of chirality: a left hand and a right hand, each holding a tetrahedral model of an amino acid (a central carbon with COOH, NH2, R and H). The two models are mirror images that cannot be superimposed, just as the hands cannot.
597109: Photographs of household sources of carboxylic acids: a bottle of wine with grapes (tartaric acid), a spilled bottle of aspirin tablets (acetylsalicylic acid), a blister pack of vitamin C tablets (ascorbic acid), lemons (citric acid) and spinach (oxalic acid).
Formic acid, H-C(=O)-OH, with the carboxyl group in red.
Acetic acid, CH3-C(=O)-OH, with the carboxyl group in red.

Ball-and-stick models of four carboxylic acids with the carboxyl group's two red oxygens visible: (a) formic acid, (b) acetic acid, (c) propionic acid and (d) butyric acid, each one carbon longer than the last.
Benzoic acid: a benzene ring attached directly to a C(=O)-OH group shown in red.

Greek-letter positions: a chain C-C-C-C-COOH with the carbons labeled delta, gamma, beta, alpha counting back from the carboxyl carbon. Below, alpha-methylpropionic acid (CH3CHCOOH with CH3 on the alpha carbon, boxed as 'the alpha carbon') and beta-hydroxybutyric acid (CH3CHCH2COOH with OH on the beta carbon, boxed as 'the beta carbon').
CH3CH2CHCOOH with Br below the carbon next to the carboxyl group.
Cl-C-C-C-COOH with the carbons numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 and lettered gamma, beta, alpha from the Cl end toward the carboxyl: the skeleton for 4-chlorobutanoic acid (gamma-chlorobutyric acid).
C-C-C-COOH with Br below carbon 2 (the alpha carbon); carbons numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 and lettered gamma, beta, alpha: the skeleton for 2-bromobutanoic acid (alpha-bromobutyric acid).
597110: RCH2OH (a primary alcohol), with [O] over the arrow, gives RCHO (an aldehyde), which with [O] gives RCOOH (a carboxylic acid).

597111: Ball-and-stick drawing of an acetic acid molecule (purple carbons, orange oxygens) surrounded by four water molecules; green dotted lines mark hydrogen bonds between the acid's carboxyl group and the water molecules.
597112: Three carboxylate salts with names: CH3COO minus Li plus, lithium acetate (lithium ethanoate); CH3CH2CH2COO minus K plus, potassium butyrate (potassium butanoate); C6H5COO minus Na plus, sodium benzoate.
CH3(CH2)14CH2COO minus Na plus, labeled 'Sodium palmitate (a soap)'.
Two food-preservative salts: (CH3CH2COO minus)2 Ca 2 plus, calcium propionate, and CH3CH=CHCH=CHCOO minus K plus, potassium sorbate.
597113: Ball-and-stick models of two esters, (a) methyl acetate and (b) ethyl acetate, each showing a carbonyl oxygen (red) and a second oxygen linking to the alkyl group.
Ethyl benzoate: a benzene ring attached to C(=O)-OCH2CH3, with the OCH2CH3 (ethyl) group in green.
CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH2CH3: an ester with an ethyl group on the carbonyl side and a four-carbon butyl group on the oxygen side.
A benzene ring attached to C(=O)-OCHCH3 with a CH3 below the CH: an ester with an isopropyl group on the oxygen.
CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH2CH3 with the CH3CH2CO (propanoate) part in red and the butyl group in green: butyl propionate (butyl propanoate).
The benzoate ester with the ring and C(=O)-O in red and the isopropyl group in green: isopropyl benzoate.
CH3CH2CH2CH2C(=O)-O- with an open bond: the pentanoate part of an ester before the alkyl group is added.
CH3CH2CH2CH2C(=O)-OCH2CH3: ethyl pentanoate, with the ethyl group attached to the oxygen.
597115: Esterification: R-C(=O)-OH plus R prime-OH (blue), with H plus over a double arrow, gives the ester R-C(=O)-OR prime plus H2O (blue).
Acetic acid, CH3-C(=O)-OH, plus 1-butanol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (blue), with H plus over a double arrow, gives butyl acetate, CH3-C(=O)-OCH2CH2CH2CH3, plus H2O.

Formation of PET: n ethylene glycol (HOCH2CH2OH) plus n terephthalic acid (a benzene ring with COOH on opposite carbons), with an arrow, gives polyethylene terephthalate, a repeating unit of a benzene ring between an ester and an OCH2CH2O link, shown in brackets with subscript n, plus n H2O.
597116: Acid hydrolysis: an ester, R-C(=O)-OR prime, plus water, with H plus over a double arrow, gives a carboxylic acid, R-C(=O)-OH, plus an alcohol, R prime-OH (blue).
Butyl acetate plus water, with H plus over a double arrow, gives acetic acid, CH3-C(=O)-OH, plus 1-butanol (butyl alcohol), CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (blue).
CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3 plus H2O, with H plus over a double arrow, gives CH3CH2CH2-C(=O)-OH plus CH3CH2OH (blue).
Saponification: an ester, R-C(=O)-OR prime, plus NaOH(aq), with an arrow, gives a carboxylate salt, R-C(=O)-ONa(aq), plus an alcohol, R prime-OH (blue).
Ethyl acetate, CH3COOCH2CH3, plus sodium hydroxide, NaOH(aq), with an arrow, gives sodium acetate, CH3-C(=O)-ONa(aq), plus ethanol (ethyl alcohol), CH3CH2OH (blue).
Methyl benzoate (a benzene ring attached to C(=O)-OCH3) plus KOH(aq), with an arrow, gives potassium benzoate (ring with C(=O)-OK) plus CH3OH (blue).
597117: Three phosphate esters with the ethyl groups in green: ethyl dihydrogen phosphate (one OCH2CH3 and two OH on P=O), diethyl hydrogen phosphate (two OCH2CH3 and one OH) and triethyl phosphate (three OCH2CH3).
Structures of phosphoric acid (one P with P=O and three OH), pyrophosphoric acid (two P units joined by an O bridge) and triphosphoric acid (three P units joined by two O bridges), each labeled.
Glycerol (three carbons, each with an OH) plus 3 HONO2 (nitric acid), with an arrow, gives glycerol trinitrate (nitroglycerin), in which each OH has become an ONO2 group, plus 3 H2O.
597118: Line-angle structure of phenol: a benzene ring with an OH group.

Acetic acid loses H plus (red curved arrows show the O-H electrons moving to O) to give the acetate ion, drawn as two resonance structures with the negative charge on either oxygen, connected by a double-headed arrow.
Ethanol loses H plus (curved arrows) to give the ethoxide ion, CH3CH2O minus, labeled 'No resonance'.

Phenol loses H plus to give the phenoxide ion, drawn as five resonance structures in which the negative charge sits on the oxygen or on the ortho and para carbons of the ring; red curved arrows show the electron movement.
Propane loses H plus from its CH3 group (curved arrows) to give a carbanion, CH3CH2CH2 minus, labeled 'No resonance'.

Four line-angle carboxylic acids meant to show how the position of a chlorine affects acidity: 2-chlorobutanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid, 4-chlorobutanoic acid and butanoic acid. (The source image prints pKa 2.83 under all four; the accepted values are about 2.8, 4.1, 4.5 and 4.8.)

Five substituted acetic acids drawn as line-angle structures with pKa values: H (acetic acid) 4.76, I 3.15, Br 2.86, Cl 2.81 and F 2.66, showing that acidity increases with the electronegativity of the substituent.
Acetic acid (CH3COOH, pKa 4.76) beside glycine drawn in its protonated form (NH3 plus-CH2-COOH, pKa 3.15), showing that the ammonium group makes the carboxylic acid stronger.

Line-angle structure of methadone hydrochloride: two phenyl rings on a quaternary carbon that bears an ethyl ketone (red O) and a branched chain ending in a dimethylammonium group (blue N-H plus) with a chloride counter-ion.

Line-angle structure of procaine hydrochloride: a benzene ring with an NH2 (blue) on one side and an ester (red O) on the other, linked through OCH2CH2 to a diethylammonium group (blue N-H plus) with a chloride counter-ion.
597121: Top row: water (H-O-H), an alcohol (R-O-H) and an ether (R-O-R prime). Bottom row: ammonia (H-N(H)-H), a primary amine (R-N(H)-H), a secondary amine (R-N(H)-R) and a tertiary amine (R-N(R)-R), showing amines as derivatives of ammonia the way alcohols and ethers derive from water.
Isopropylamine, CH3CHCH3 with NH2 (blue) on the middle carbon, labeled 'a primary amine', beside isopropyl alcohol, CH3CHCH3 with OH (green) on the middle carbon, labeled 'a secondary alcohol'.
CH3CH2NCH3 with a CH3 below the N: a tertiary amine (ethyldimethylamine).
CH3CHNHCH3 with a CH3 below the CH: isopropylmethylamine, a secondary amine.
CH3CH2NCH2CH3 with a CH3 below the N: diethylmethylamine, a tertiary amine.
CH3CH2NCH3 (ethyl in red, methyl in green) with a CH3 (green) below the N: ethyldimethylamine, with the groups color-coded for naming.

Aniline (a benzene ring with NH2), m-chloroaniline (NH2 and Cl separated by one ring carbon) and 2-chloro-4-iodoaniline (NH2 with Cl on the adjacent carbon and I on the carbon opposite), each labeled.
A benzene ring with an NH2 group and a Br separated by one ring carbon (meta).
A benzene ring with an NH2 group and a Cl on adjacent carbons (ortho).
A benzene ring with H2N on one carbon and CH2CH3 on the opposite carbon: p-ethylaniline.
CH3CH-CHCH3 with NH2 below the second carbon and CH3 below the third: 3-methyl-2-butanamine.
The amine functional group drawn three ways: -NH2 (primary), -NH- with two open bonds (secondary), 'or' -N with three open bonds (tertiary); each N shows its lone pair.
597122: Ball-and-stick drawings: (a) two amine molecules (purple N, blue H) linked by a green dotted hydrogen bond from one N-H to the lone pair of the other N; (b) an amine molecule hydrogen-bonded to three water molecules (orange O).
beta-Naphthylamine: two fused benzene rings (naphthalene) with an NH2 group on the second carbon.
597123: A tertiary amine R3N (N in blue) plus H2O gives, in equilibrium, a substituted ammonium ion [R3NH] plus in brackets plus OH minus.
Methylamine, CH3NH2(aq), plus H2O gives, in equilibrium, the methylammonium ion, CH3NH3 plus(aq), plus OH minus(aq).
Octylamine (insoluble), CH3(CH2)7NH2(l), plus HNO3(aq), with an arrow, gives octylammonium nitrate (soluble), CH3(CH2)7NH3 plus NO3 minus(aq).
Structure of caffeine: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, containing four nitrogen atoms, three of which carry CH3 groups, and two C=O groups.
Structure of nicotine: a pyridine ring (six-membered aromatic ring with one N) attached to a five-membered pyrrolidine ring whose N carries a CH3 group.
Structure of cocaine: a bicyclic ring system with an N-CH3 bridge, bearing a methyl ester (C(=O)-OCH3) and a benzoate ester (O-C(=O)-phenyl).
597124: The amide group, C(=O)-N with open bonds, shown in green; a simple amide, C(=O)-NH2; and a substituted amide, C(=O)-NH-R.
Formic acid (methanoic acid), H-C(=O)-OH with the carboxyl in red, beside formamide (methanamide), H-C(=O)-NH2 with the amide group in green.
Benzamide: a benzene ring attached to C(=O)-NH2.
The amide functional group: a carbonyl carbon bonded to a nitrogen, with open bonds on the carbon and on the nitrogen.
597125: Hydrogen bonding in amides: (a) an acetamide molecule hydrogen-bonded (dotted lines) to two water molecules through its C=O oxygen and its N-H hydrogen; (b) two acetamide molecules linked by a dotted hydrogen bond from the N-H of one to the C=O of the other.
597126: Acetic acid, CH3COOH, plus NH3, with an arrow, gives acetamide, CH3CONH2, plus H2O.
Formation of nylon 66: n H2N(CH2)6NH2 (1,6-hexanediamine) plus n HOOC(CH2)4COOH (adipic acid), with an arrow, gives the polyamide repeating unit -[NH(CH2)6NHCO(CH2)4CO]n- plus 2n H2O.
597127: Acetamide, CH3-C(=O)-NH2, plus H2O, with 'enzymes' over the arrow, gives acetic acid, CH3-C(=O)-OH, plus NH3.
Butanamide, CH3CH2CH2-C(=O)-NH2, plus H2O, with an arrow, gives butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2-C(=O)-OH, plus NH3.
Benzamide (a benzene ring with C(=O)-NH2) plus H2O, with an arrow, gives benzoic acid (ring with C(=O)-OH) plus NH3.
597128: Structure of caffeine: a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, containing four nitrogen atoms, three of which carry CH3 groups, and two C=O groups.
Structure of nicotine: a pyridine ring (six-membered aromatic ring with one N) attached to a five-membered pyrrolidine ring whose N carries a CH3 group.
Structure of cocaine: a bicyclic ring system with an N-CH3 bridge, bearing a methyl ester (C(=O)-OCH3) and a benzoate ester (O-C(=O)-phenyl), labeled 'Cocaine'.
C17H21O4N (cocaine, freebase) plus HCl, with an arrow, gives C17H21O4NH plus Cl minus (cocaine hydrochloride).
597129: Line-angle structures of four alkaloids: nicotine (pyridine ring plus N-methylpyrrolidine), morphine (a five-ring fused system with two OH groups and an N-CH3), codeine (the same skeleton with one OH replaced by OCH3) and heroin (the same skeleton with both OH groups converted to acetate esters), each labeled.
Photograph of a field of red poppies in bloom.
597130: Nylon synthesis: adipic acid (HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH) plus hexanediamine (H2N-(CH2)6-NH2), with an arrow, give nylon-66, drawn as a repeating unit in brackets with an amide link (C(=O)-NH) joining the two building blocks.
Photograph of a black nylon kitchen spatula.
The repeating unit of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) in brackets with subscript n: a benzene ring between two ester groups, linked through O-CH2-CH2-O.
597134: Fischer projection of glucose with the aldehyde functional group (H-C=O at the top, in blue, boxed and labeled) and the OH groups on the other carbons in red; a note says that because glucose has an aldehyde group and several OH groups it is a polyhydroxy aldehyde.
A three-carbon sugar: CH=O at the top, a middle carbon with HO on the left and H on the right, and CH2OH at the bottom (an aldotriose).
CH2OH at the top, a middle carbon with H on the left and OH on the right, CH2OH at the bottom: not a carbohydrate by the aldehyde or ketone test (glycerol).
CH2OH at the top, C=O in the middle, CH2OH at the bottom: dihydroxyacetone, a ketotriose.
CH3 at the top, C=O in the middle, CH2OH at the bottom: hydroxyacetone, which has a ketone but only one OH.
A four-carbon chain: CH2OH, C=O, CH2, CH2OH from top to bottom; a ketone with OH groups only at the ends.
A four-carbon aldose: CH=O at the top, HO-C-H, H-C-OH, CH2OH at the bottom (an aldotetrose).
A four-carbon ketose: CH2OH, C=O, H-C-OH, CH2OH from top to bottom (a ketotetrose).
A four-carbon chain: CH2OH, H-C-OH, CH2, CH2OH from top to bottom; a polyol with no aldehyde or ketone group.
597135: Fischer projections of glucose (an aldohexose) with the H-C=O aldehyde at the top in blue and OH groups right, left, right, right on carbons 2 to 5, and fructose (a ketohexose) with CH2OH at the top, a C=O in blue on carbon 2, and OH groups left, right, right on carbons 3 to 5; both end in CH2OH.
Fischer projection of a ketopentose: CH2OH at the top, C=O on carbon 2, H-C-OH, HO-C-H, and CH2OH at the bottom.
Fischer projection of an aldotetrose: H-C=O at the top, HO-C-H, HO-C-H, and CH2OH at the bottom.

(a) Fischer projections of the trioses: D-(+)-glyceraldehyde (CHO at the top, OH on the right of the middle carbon in red, CH2OH at the bottom), L-(-)-glyceraldehyde (the same with OH on the left) and dihydroxyacetone (CH2OH, C=O, CH2OH). (b) Photograph of ball-and-stick models of the two glyceraldehyde enantiomers beside a mirror.

Diagram of polarized light: (a) a light bulb emitting light with waves vibrating in all directions, shown as a circle full of lines; (b) after passing through a polarizer the circle shows only one line, and a second polarizer at right angles shows the light vibrating in the perpendicular plane.
Two photographs of a sheet of polarizing film over a light: when a second sheet is aligned with it the light passes (left); when rotated 90 degrees the overlap is dark (right).
Cutaway diagram of a polarimeter: a light source, a Nicol prism (polarizer), a sample tube, a second Nicol prism (analyzer) on a circular scale that reads the angle of rotation, and an eyepiece.
597136: Fischer projections of D-(+)-glucose, D-(+)-galactose and D-(-)-fructose, each above a photograph of a food source: fruit for glucose, a glass of milk for galactose, and jars of honey for fructose.
Fischer projection of D-glucose with the carbons numbered 1 to 6 in red: carbon 1 is the aldehyde H-C=O, carbons 2, 4 and 5 have OH on the right, carbon 3 has OH on the left, and carbon 6 is CH2OH.

Structures of five artificial sweeteners, each labeled: saccharin (a fused ring with SO2 and C=O around an N minus Na plus), cyclamate (a cyclohexane ring with NH-SO3 minus Na plus), aspartame (a dipeptide of aspartic acid and the methyl ester of phenylalanine), acesulfame K (a six-membered ring containing N minus K plus, SO2 and C=O) and sucralose (a sucrose skeleton with three Cl atoms replacing OH groups).
597137: Hemiacetal formation: an aldehyde, R-CH=O, plus an alcohol, R prime-OH (blue), gives in equilibrium a carbon bearing OH and OR prime (blue), R and H. Below, a ketone, R-C(=O)-R prime, plus an alcohol R double-prime-OH gives a carbon bearing OH, OR double-prime, R and R prime (a hemiketal).

Cyclization of D-glucose in three panels: (a) the Fischer projection with carbons numbered 1 to 6; (b) a three-dimensional representation in which the chain curls so the OH on carbon 5 approaches the aldehyde carbon 1 (curved arrow); (c) the resulting six-membered ring (Haworth projection) with the ring oxygen and the new OH on carbon 1.

Equilibrium mixtures of two monosaccharides as Haworth projections. (a) alpha-D-(+)-glucose (OH on carbon 1 pointing down) in equilibrium with the open-chain D-(+)-glucose aldehyde, in equilibrium with beta-D-(+)-glucose (OH on carbon 1 pointing up). (b) alpha-D-(-)-fructose, the open-chain ketone D-(-)-fructose, and beta-D-(-)-fructose, each a five-membered ring.
597138: Two oxidation tests on an aldose (H-C=O with an R group). Top: aldose plus Ag(NH3)2 plus (Tollens' reagent, clear solution), with an arrow, gives a carboxylate anion plus Ag(s), silver. Bottom: aldose plus Cu(citrate)2 2 minus (Benedict's reagent, blue solution) gives a carboxylate anion plus Cu2O(s), a brick-red precipitate.
Photograph of three test tubes after Benedict's test: the first two contain a brick-red precipitate (positive, reducing sugars) and the third is still clear blue (negative).
597139: Formation of maltose: two alpha-D-(+)-glucose rings (monosaccharides), with the anomeric carbon and the alcohol OH labeled, plus H plus over the arrow, join through an alpha-1,4-glycosidic linkage (circled in red) to give alpha-maltose (a disaccharide) plus H2O; a note says the orientation of the OH on the anomeric carbon identifies the disaccharide as alpha-maltose.

Equilibrium mixture of maltose isomers: alpha-maltose (two glucose rings joined by an alpha-1,4-glycosidic linkage, with the free anomeric OH in the alpha orientation) and beta-maltose (the same with the free anomeric OH in the beta orientation), both in equilibrium with the open-chain aldehyde intermediate shown below.

Hydrolysis of lactose: alpha-D-lactose, a galactose ring joined to a glucose ring by a beta-1,4-glycosidic linkage (red), with 'H plus or lactase' over the arrow, gives D-galactose plus D-glucose; a note explains the convention of writing the anomeric OH with a wavy bond when the alpha or beta form is not specified.

A trisaccharide of three six-membered rings numbered 1, 2 and 3, joined by two glycosidic O links; the OH groups at the linkages point down (alpha) from ring 1 and up (beta) from ring 2, and ring 3 has a free anomeric OH.

A trisaccharide of three six-membered rings numbered 1, 2 and 3, joined by two glycosidic O links; the linking O from ring 1 points up (beta) and from ring 2 points down (alpha), and ring 3 has a free anomeric OH.

Formation of sucrose: alpha-D-glucose (six-membered ring) plus beta-D-fructose (five-membered ring), with an arrow, give sucrose plus H2O; the two rings are joined through an alpha-1,beta-2-glycosidic linkage (bracketed in blue) between the two anomeric carbons.
597140: Amylose: (a) a chain of four glucose rings in Haworth form joined by alpha-1,4 linkages (labeled), continuing 'etc.' at both ends; (b) a drawing of the chain coiled into a helix with the glucose units shown as small rings along the coil.
Amylopectin: a branched tree of glucose chains; a circular inset magnifies a branch point showing alpha-1,4 linkages along a chain and an alpha-1,6 linkage joining a side chain.
Cellulose: (a) two parallel chains of beta-linked glucose units with dotted lines showing hydrogen bonds between the chains; (b) a micrograph of cellulose fibers.
Photograph of a diabetes educator in a white coat talking with visitors at an information table covered with food models and pamphlets.
597144: A cis fatty acid, with the two H atoms on the same side of the C=C and the chain segments CH3(CH2)5 and (CH2)7COOH on the other side, beside a trans fatty acid, with the H atoms on opposite sides of the double bond.

Arachidonic acid (a twenty-carbon chain with four cis double bonds and a COOH) reacts with 2 O2 under the enzyme cyclooxygenase to give the cyclic prostaglandin PGH2; arrows lead to PGD2 (critical to the development of allergic diseases such as asthma) and PGE2 (used to induce labor), each a five-membered ring bearing two side chains.

The structure of a saturated fatty acid: (a) a ball-and-stick model of a straight chain of black carbon atoms with hydrogens, ending in a red carboxyl group; (b) a space-filling model of the same straight chain.

Myricyl cerotate (found in carnauba wax): CH3(CH2)24-C(=O)-O-(CH2)29CH3, with the CH3(CH2)24C(=O) part labeled 'from a fatty acid' in blue and the O(CH2)29CH3 part labeled 'from a long-chain alcohol'.
597145: Three fatty acids (RCOOH, R prime COOH, R double-prime COOH, in blue) plus glycerol (a three-carbon chain with an OH on each carbon), with 'catalyst' over the arrow, give a triglyceride in which each glycerol carbon carries an ester O-C(=O)-R group, plus 3 H2O.
Tristearin, a simple triglyceride: a glycerol backbone whose three carbons each carry an ester O-C(=O)-CH2(CH2)15CH3 (three identical stearate chains, in blue).
A mixed triglyceride: a glycerol backbone with three different ester chains: CH2(CH2)11CH3 (blue), CH2(CH2)13CH3 (pink) and (CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7CH3 (red, an oleate chain with one double bond).
Diacetyl, CH3-C(=O)-C(=O)-CH3, and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone, CH3-C(=O)-CH(OH)-CH3, the butter-flavor compounds.

Soap making: a triglyceride (glycerol esterified with three C15H31 fatty acid chains) plus H2O, with 'heat, pressure' over the arrow, gives glycerol plus 2 CH3(CH2)14COOH plus CH3(CH2)16COOH (hydrolysis of triglycerides produces fatty acids); these react with NaOH to give the sodium carboxylate soap molecules.

A soap micelle: a sphere of soap molecules with their hydrocarbon chains (nonpolar and hydrophobic) pointing inward and their ionic ends (polar and hydrophilic) on the surface, surrounded by water molecules.
Hydrogenation of a C=C in a fatty acid: a carbon-carbon double bond with two H atoms plus H2 (red), with an arrow, gives a single bond with two added H atoms (red).
The readily oxidized unit in polyunsaturated fatty acids: ~CH=CH-CH2-CH=CH~, a CH2 between two double bonds, with the two carbons that are attacked shown in red.
Malonaldehyde: H-C(=O)-CH2-C(=O)-H, with the two carbonyl carbons in red.
597146: Line-angle structure of a phosphatidylcholine: two long fatty acid chains (one with a cis double bond) esterified to a glycerol backbone whose third carbon carries a phosphate linked to choline, O-CH2CH2-N(CH3)3 plus.
Space-filling model of a phospholipid: two long gray-and-white hydrocarbon tails and a compact head group with red oxygens, an orange phosphorus and a blue nitrogen.

Condensed structure of a phosphatidylcholine: glycerol carbon 1 esterified to palmitate ((CH2)14CH3), carbon 2 esterified to oleate ((CH2)7CH=CH(CH2)7CH3), and carbon 3 bonded through O to a phosphate (P in red) that links to O(CH2)2N(CH3)3 plus.

A phospholipid space-filling model with its regions labeled: a polar head made of choline (blue), phosphate (red) and glycerol (yellow), and a non-polar tail made of a palmitic acid chain and an oleic acid chain (gray).

Line-angle structure of 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl phosphatidylcholine (a lecithin): a glycerol backbone with a saturated palmitate chain, an oleate chain with one cis double bond, and a phosphate (red) bonded to choline (blue N plus with three methyl groups).

Structure of flavin adenine dinucleotide: the oxidized form FAD (a three-ring flavin attached through ribitol and two phosphates to ribose and adenine) plus 2 H plus and 2 electrons gives the reduced form FADH2, in which the flavin ring (red) has gained two hydrogens.

A four-carbon dicarboxylate with a CH2-CH2 single bond plus FAD, with 'Succinate dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives the same dicarboxylate with a CH=CH double bond plus FADH2. (The source image labels the reactant 'Fumarate' and the product 'Succinate'; the names are reversed: succinate is oxidized to fumarate.)

Structure of coenzyme A divided by dashed lines into five numbered parts: 1, 3 prime-phosphoadenosine (adenine on a ribose with a phosphate on carbon 3 prime); 2, a diphosphate; 3, pantoic acid (a branched chain with two methyls and an OH); 4, beta-alanine linked by an amide; 5, cysteamine, ending in the free SH group.
Pyruvate, CH3-C(=O)-COO minus, plus HS-CoA plus NAD plus, with 'Pyruvate dehydrogenase' over the arrow, gives acetyl CoA, CH3-C(=O)-S-CoA, plus CO2 plus NADH.
Acetyl CoA, CH3-C(=O)-S-CoA, plus HS-ACP (acyl carrier protein), with an arrow, gives acetyl ACP, CH3-C(=O)-S-ACP, plus HS-CoA (not shown).

Active site of malate dehydrogenase: the substrate malate (highlighted in pink) is held by hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions with the side chains of Arg102, Arg109, Arg171, Asp168 and His195, while the nicotinamide ring of NAD plus sits below it ready to accept a hydride.

Three panels showing enzyme action in citrate synthase: oxaloacetate binds in the active site, acetyl CoA adds to its carbonyl to form citryl CoA, and hydrolysis releases citrate and CoA-SH; active-site residues are drawn in blue around the substrates.
597189: Structure of adenosine triphosphate (ATP): an adenine base attached to a ribose (with 2 prime and 3 prime OH groups), whose 5 prime CH2 carries a chain of three phosphate groups.
Two phosphate groups joined through an oxygen, with the P-O-P anhydride bond drawn as a red wavy line to mark it as a high-energy bond.
Hydrolysis of ATP: adenosine triphosphate plus H2O, with an arrow, gives adenosine diphosphate (ADP) plus a phosphate ion plus energy (red).
An acyl phosphate: R-C(=O)-O-PO3 2 minus, with the bond between the carboxyl oxygen and phosphorus drawn as a red wavy line (a high-energy bond).
A guanidine phosphate: R-NH-C(=NH)-NH-PO3 2 minus, with the N-P bond drawn as a red wavy line (a high-energy bond).
A pyrophosphate: R-O-PO2 minus-O-PO3 2 minus, with the P-O-P anhydride bond drawn as a red wavy line (a high-energy bond).
A sugar phosphate: R-O-PO3 2 minus, with the O-P ester bond drawn as a red wavy line (a lower-energy phosphate bond).
597190: Labeled diagram of the human digestive system: salivary glands, oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, liver, gallbladder, common bile duct, duodenum, stomach, pancreas, pancreatic duct, small intestine (jejunum, ileum), colon (ascending, transverse, descending), cecum, appendix, rectum and anus.
597191: Flowchart of energy conversions in catabolism: Stage 1, proteins, carbohydrates and fats are hydrolyzed to amino acids, monosaccharides and fatty acids and glycerol; Stage 2, these are converted to acetyl CoA (or pyruvate), with some ATP made; Stage 3, acetyl CoA enters the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain, producing most of the ATP, with CO2 and H2O released.

The principal events and sites of carbohydrate digestion: in the mouth, salivary alpha-amylase begins breaking dietary carbohydrates into polysaccharides, dextrins and disaccharides; in the stomach nothing further happens; in the small intestine pancreatic alpha-amylase and intestinal enzymes give monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose), which are absorbed by active transport through the intestinal lining into the bloodstream.

The principal events and sites of protein digestion: in the mouth nothing happens; in the stomach HCl and pepsin denature and partially hydrolyze proteins; in the small intestine trypsin, chymotrypsin, aminopeptidase and carboxypeptidase give small peptides and amino acids, which are absorbed by active transport through the intestinal lining into the blood.

Activation of pancreatic enzymes: enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen to trypsin; trypsin then converts more trypsinogen to trypsin and converts chymotrypsinogen to chymotrypsin (dashed arrows show the activations).

A short peptide drawn out with the peptide bonds that each enzyme cleaves marked in red: aminopeptidase at the N-terminal bond, pepsin next to aromatic residues, chymotrypsin or pepsin next to phenylalanine, trypsin next to lysine, and carboxypeptidase at the C-terminal bond.

The principal events and sites of lipid digestion: in the mouth and stomach dietary lipids (mostly triglycerides) are only physically broken up into droplets in chyme; in the small intestine bile salts emulsify the fat and pancreatic lipase partially hydrolyzes it to mono- and diglycerides in micelles, which are absorbed through the intestinal lining and repackaged into chylomicrons for transport in the blood.

A triglyceride (glycerol with three fatty acid esters) plus H2O, with 'lipase' over the arrow, gives a diglyceride plus a fatty acid (R-COOH); a second lipase step gives a monoglyceride (one ester left on the middle carbon) plus another fatty acid.
597192: The preparatory phase of glycolysis as a flowchart with structures: glucose is phosphorylated by hexokinase (1, using ATP) to glucose 6-phosphate, isomerized by phosphoglucose isomerase (2) to fructose 6-phosphate, phosphorylated by phosphofructokinase-1 (3, using ATP) to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, split by aldolase (4) into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate, which triose phosphate isomerase (5) interconverts.

The payoff phase of glycolysis as a flowchart with structures: two glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate are oxidized by glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (6, with 2 NAD plus giving 2 NADH) to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; phosphoglycerate kinase (7) makes 2 ATP and gives 3-phosphoglycerate; phosphoglycerate mutase (8) gives 2-phosphoglycerate; enolase (9) removes water to give phosphoenolpyruvate; and pyruvate kinase (10) makes 2 more ATP and gives pyruvate.

Structures of oral antidiabetic drugs: first-generation sulfonylureas tolbutamide (Orinase) and chlorpropamide (Diabinese), each a benzene ring bearing a sulfonylurea chain, and the second-generation drug glyburide (Diabeta, Glynase or Micronase), a larger molecule with an additional substituted benzamide and a cyclohexyl group.

The metabolic fates of pyruvate: glucose 6-phosphate forms pyruvate by glycolysis (and the reverse by gluconeogenesis); pyruvate goes to acetyl-CoA under aerobic conditions, to lactate under anaerobic conditions in vertebrates, or to ethanol under anaerobic conditions in microorganisms.
597193: The ten steps of glycolysis drawn as a pathway with structures: glucose to glucose 6-phosphate (hexokinase), fructose 6-phosphate (phosphoglucose isomerase), fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase), splitting by aldolase into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (interconverted by triose phosphate isomerase), then 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, 3-phosphoglycerate, 2-phosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate and pyruvate, with each enzyme and the ATP, ADP, NAD plus and NADH used or made marked.
Glucose (a six-membered ring) plus ATP, with 'Hexokinase' over the arrow and ADP released, gives glucose 6-phosphate, the ring with a phosphate on its CH2 group.
Glucose 6-phosphate (a six-membered ring), with 'Phosphohexose isomerase' over a double arrow, gives fructose 6-phosphate (a five-membered ring with a CH2OH and a phosphorylated CH2).
Fructose 6-phosphate plus ATP, with 'Phosphofructokinase-1' over the arrow and ADP released, gives fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, a five-membered ring with phosphates on both CH2 groups.

Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, with 'Aldolase' over the arrow, splits into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (a three-carbon ketone with a phosphate) plus glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (a three-carbon aldehyde with a phosphate).
Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (CH2O-phosphate, C=O, CH2OH), with 'Triosephosphate isomerase' over a double arrow, gives glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (CHO, H-C-OH, CH2O-phosphate).

Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate plus NAD plus and inorganic phosphate (Pi), with 'Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase' over the arrow and NADH plus H plus released, gives 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which has a phosphate on the carboxyl (an acyl phosphate) and one on carbon 3.
1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate plus ADP, with 'Phosphoglycerate kinase' over the arrow and ATP released, gives 3-phosphoglycerate, a carboxylate with a phosphate on carbon 3.
3-Phosphoglycerate (phosphate on carbon 3), with 'Phosphoglycerate mutase' over a double arrow, gives 2-phosphoglycerate (phosphate on carbon 2, CH2OH on carbon 3).
2-Phosphoglycerate, with 'Enolase' over a double arrow, loses H2O to give phosphoenolpyruvate, which has a C=CH2 double bond and a phosphate on carbon 2.
Phosphoenolpyruvate plus ADP, with 'Pyruvate kinase' over the arrow and ATP released, gives enolpyruvate (C=CH2 with an OH), which rearranges to pyruvate (C=O with a CH3).
Photograph of two women jogging side by side.

Fermentation: pyruvate (CH3-C(=O)-COO minus) loses CO2 (pink) under pyruvate decarboxylase (with TPP and Mg 2 plus) to give acetaldehyde, CH3CH=O, which alcohol dehydrogenase reduces with NADH plus H plus (giving NAD plus) to ethanol, CH3CH2OH.
597200: The structure of acetyl-coenzyme A with its parts bracketed: the acetyl group (CH3-C(=O)-, red) joined through a thioester to the sulfur of coenzyme A, whose chain contains pantothenic acid (a vitamin) and a phosphorylated ADP ending in adenine.

Flowchart of acetyl-CoA's roles: acetyl-CoA (CH3-C(=O)-SCoA) feeds the citric acid cycle, is built into fatty acids and then triglycerides, and combines to form acetoacetyl-CoA, which leads to cholesterol (and from it other steroids and bile salts) and to ketone bodies.

The ten-step glycolysis pathway drawn in a loop with structures: glucose to G6P (hexokinase, 1), F6P (PGI, 2), F1,6BP (PFK, 3), split by aldolase (4) into GADP and DHAP (TPI, 5), then 1,3BPG (GAPDH, 6), 3PG (PGK, 7), 2PG (PGM, 8), PEP (enolase, 9) and pyruvate (PK, 10); the atoms that change in each step are highlighted in pink or yellow.
Space-filling model of a triglyceride: three long chains of black carbon and white hydrogen spheres attached through red oxygen atoms to a glycerol backbone, two chains folded back on the third.
Ball-and-stick model of glycerol: three gray carbon atoms in a chain, each bonded to a red oxygen with its white hydrogen, on a blue background.

Line-angle structures of trans-oleic acid (an eighteen-carbon chain with a trans double bond, nearly straight) and cis-oleic acid (the same chain with a cis double bond that puts a sharp bend in it), each with a COOH at the left end.

Beta-oxidation step 1: an acyl-CoA (R-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-S-CoA) with FAD giving FADH2 over the arrow, catalyzed by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, gives trans-delta-2-enoyl-CoA, which has a trans C=C between the alpha and beta carbons.
Beta-oxidation step 2: trans-delta-2-enoyl-CoA plus H2O, catalyzed by enoyl-CoA hydratase, gives L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA, with an OH on the beta carbon.
Beta-oxidation step 3: L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA with NAD plus giving NADH plus H plus over the arrow, catalyzed by hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, gives 3-ketoacyl-CoA, with a C=O on the beta carbon.
Beta-oxidation step 4: 3-ketoacyl-CoA plus CoA-SH, catalyzed by thiolase, gives a shortened acyl-CoA (R-C(=O)-S-CoA) plus acetyl-CoA (CH3-C(=O)-S-CoA).
597201: The citric acid cycle drawn as a circle of structures with enzymes numbered 1 to 8: acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate (citrate synthase) to make citrate; aconitase gives isocitrate; isocitrate dehydrogenase releases CO2 and makes NADH, giving alpha-ketoglutarate; the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex releases CO2 and makes NADH, giving succinyl-CoA; succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP, giving succinate; succinate dehydrogenase makes FADH2, giving fumarate; fumarase adds water, giving malate; and malate dehydrogenase makes NADH, regenerating oxaloacetate. NADH, FADH2, GTP and CO2 are highlighted.

Succinyl-CoA plus H2O, with 'Succinyl-CoA synthetase' over a double arrow and Pi plus GDP giving GTP, gives succinate plus coenzyme A; below, GTP plus ADP, with 'nucleoside diphosphokinase', gives GDP plus ATP.
Cutaway drawing of a mitochondrion with the outer membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae, intermembrane space, matrix and DNA labeled.

The mitochondrial electron transport chain in the inner membrane: complexes I, II, III and IV and ATP synthase drawn between the intermembrane space (top, with many H plus ions) and the matrix (bottom). A red line traces electrons from NADH (at complex I) and from FADH2 (at complex II) through the chain to O2, which becomes H2O at complex IV; H plus pumped into the intermembrane space flows back through ATP synthase to make ATP from ADP plus Pi.
Oxidation half-reaction: L-malate (minus OOC-CH2-CH(OH)-COO minus, with the OH and H in blue) gives oxaloacetate (minus OOC-CH2-C(=O)-COO minus) plus 2 H plus plus 2 electrons.

Reduction half-reaction: NAD plus (a nicotinamide ring with a positive nitrogen and a C(=O)NH2 group, attached to R) plus 2 H plus plus 2 electrons gives NADH (the ring has gained a hydrogen, shown in blue, and lost its charge) plus H plus.
Oxidation half-reaction: NADH plus H plus, with an arrow, gives NAD plus plus 2 H plus plus 2 electrons (the H and electrons in blue).

Reduction of flavin mononucleotide: FMN (a three-ring flavin with two methyl groups, attached to R) plus 2 H plus plus 2 electrons gives FMNH2, in which two ring nitrogens have gained hydrogens (blue).

Reduction of coenzyme Q: the quinone ring of coenzyme Q (two C=O groups, two OCH3 groups, a methyl and a long isoprenoid side chain) plus 2 H plus plus 2 electrons gives coenzyme QH2, the hydroquinone with two OH groups.

An iron porphyrin (heme): four pyrrole rings joined into a large ring around a central Fe 2 plus (red) bonded to the four nitrogens; the ring bears methyl, vinyl (CH=CH2) and propionate (CH2CH2COO minus) side chains.
597202: The citric acid cycle drawn as a circle of structures with enzymes numbered 1 to 8: acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate (citrate synthase) to make citrate; aconitase gives isocitrate; isocitrate dehydrogenase releases CO2 and makes NADH, giving alpha-ketoglutarate; the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex releases CO2 and makes NADH, giving succinyl-CoA; succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP, giving succinate; succinate dehydrogenase makes FADH2, giving fumarate; fumarase adds water, giving malate; and malate dehydrogenase makes NADH, regenerating oxaloacetate.

Oxaloacetate (blue: COO minus, C=O, CH2, COO minus) plus acetyl-CoA (red CH3-C(=O)-S-CoA), with H2O over the arrow, gives citrate, in which the acetyl carbon (red) has added to the keto carbon to make a tertiary alcohol carbon bearing OH and three carboxylate-containing arms, plus CoA-SH.

Citrate (with the OH and an H highlighted in red) loses H2O to give the intermediate cis-aconitate (a C=C bearing three carboxylates), which adds H2O back the other way to give isocitrate, with the OH (red) now on a different carbon.

Mechanism of isocitrate dehydrogenase: isocitrate's secondary OH is oxidized by NAD(P) plus (hydride transfer to the nicotinamide ring, blue) to give intermediate I (a keto acid held by Mg 2 plus), which loses CO2 to give an enol intermediate II that is protonated by H-A to give alpha-ketoglutarate.
alpha-Ketoglutarate (COO minus, CH2, CH2, C=O, COO minus) plus CoA-SH and NAD plus, with an arrow and CO2 plus NADH plus H plus released, gives succinyl-CoA (COO minus, CH2, CH2, C(=O)-SCoA).
Succinyl-CoA plus GDP and Pi, with an arrow and GTP plus CoA-SH released, gives succinate (COO minus, CH2, CH2, COO minus).
Succinate (COO minus, CH2, CH2, COO minus) with FAD giving FADH2 over the arrow gives fumarate, a trans C=C with a COO minus and an H on each carbon.
Fumarate plus H2O, with an arrow, gives (S)-malate: COO minus, HO-C-H, CH2, COO minus.
Malate (COO minus, HO-C-H, CH2, COO minus) with NAD plus giving NADH plus H plus over the arrow gives oxaloacetate (COO minus, C=O, CH2, COO minus).

In the matrix the citric acid cycle produces NADH and succinate, which feed complexes I to IV in the inner membrane; the complexes pump H plus out of the matrix and pass electrons to O2 to make H2O, and ATP synthase lets H plus flow back in to convert ADP plus Pi to ATP.

Flavin mononucleotide: the oxidized form FMN (a three-ring flavin attached to a ribitol chain ending in a phosphate) plus 2 H plus and 2 electrons (red arrows show where they add) gives the reduced form FMNH2, with two new N-H hydrogens shown in blue.

Ubiquinone (Q), a quinone ring with two OCH3 groups, a methyl and a ten-unit isoprenoid tail, gains one electron to give the semiubiquinone radical anion (Q dot minus), or 2 electrons plus 2 H plus to give ubiquinol (QH2), the ring with two OH groups.
The heme of cytochrome c: an iron atom at the center of a porphyrin ring with methyl, propionic acid (CH2CH2COOH) and thioether (CH(CH3)-SH) side chains that attach it to the protein.

Complex II: succinate is oxidized to fumarate plus 2 H plus, reducing FAD to FADH2; the electrons pass through Fe-S centers and a heme to reduce Q to QH2. No protons are pumped.

Complex III (the Q cycle) in two steps: in step 1, QH2 gives one electron to cytochrome c (oxidized to reduced) and one to Q, releasing 2 H plus; in step 2 a second QH2 does the same and the Q radical takes up 2 H plus to regenerate QH2.

Complex IV: four reduced cytochrome c molecules each give one electron, which pass through a copper center and two iron (heme) centers to a second copper, reducing O2 plus 4 H plus to 2 H2O while 4 H plus are pumped across the membrane.
ATP synthase in the inner membrane: H plus flows from the intermembrane space (pink, top) through the enzyme into the matrix (blue, bottom), driving the conversion of ADP plus Pi into ATP plus H2O.

Molecular surface model of ATP synthase: the membrane-embedded Fo part (red) below and the F1 head (blue, teal and purple subunits) above, with the position of the inner membrane of mitochondria (or gram-negative bacteria) marked.

Cartoon of ATP synthase with its parts labeled: the F1 head (alpha-beta subunits, green) holding ATP, the central gamma stalk (F1 gamma), the ring of Fo c subunits (purple) in the membrane, and the Fo a and Fo b subunits forming the stator.

Step a of c-ring rotation: a red plus (the proton-binding site on the stator) sits beside c-subunit 1, which carries a blue minus (an empty, charged binding site); subunit 2 is next in line.

Step h: subunit 1 releases its proton to the inside (red H plus labeled 'innen', inside), leaving a blue minus site.

Dicumarol: two 4-hydroxycoumarin units (each a benzene ring fused to a lactone ring bearing an OH) joined by a CH2 bridge.

597208: Transamination: an amino acid (R-CH(NH3 plus)-COO minus, with the amino group in blue) plus an alpha-keto acid (R prime-C(=O)-COO minus), with 'transaminase' over a double arrow, gives a new alpha-keto acid (R-C(=O)-COO minus) plus a new amino acid (R prime-CH(NH3 plus)-COO minus).

Two transamination reactions: (a) alanine plus alpha-ketoglutarate, with 'glutamate-pyruvate transaminase', gives pyruvate plus glutamate; (b) aspartate plus alpha-ketoglutarate, with 'glutamate-oxaloacetate transaminase', gives oxaloacetate plus glutamate. The amino groups are shown in blue.
Oxidative deamination: glutamate plus H2O, with 'glutamate dehydrogenase' over a double arrow and NAD plus converted to NADH plus H plus, gives alpha-ketoglutarate plus NH4 plus.

Fates of the carbon skeletons of amino acids: boxes of amino acid names point to where they enter the citric acid cycle or glycolysis. Alanine, cysteine, glycine, serine, threonine and tryptophan enter as pyruvate; isoleucine, leucine and tryptophan as acetyl CoA; leucine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and tyrosine as acetoacetyl CoA; arginine, glutamate, glutamine, histidine and proline as alpha-ketoglutarate; isoleucine, methionine and valine as succinyl-CoA; aspartate, phenylalanine and tyrosine as fumarate; asparagine and aspartate as oxaloacetate, which can lead through phosphoenolpyruvate to glucose (red).
Photograph of a person walking on a treadmill wearing a breathing mask connected by tubing to a cart of monitoring equipment, in an ergospirometry laboratory.
597209: Terms used in fatty acid oxidation: a fatty acid, R-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-OH, with its alpha and beta carbons labeled; an acyl-CoA, R-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-S-CoA; and acetyl-CoA, H3C-C(=O)-S-CoA; the carbonyl groups are in red.
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) reacts with a fatty acid carboxylate (the acylate attacks the alpha phosphate, red arrow) to give acyl adenylate (R-C(=O)-O-PO2 minus-O-Ad) plus pyrophosphate (PPi).
Acyl adenylate plus minus S-CoA, with an arrow, gives acyl-CoA (R-C(=O)-SCoA) plus adenosine monophosphate (AMP).
Beta-oxidation step 1: acyl-CoA (R-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-S-CoA) with FAD giving FADH2 over the arrow, catalyzed by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, gives trans-delta-2-enoyl-CoA.
Beta-oxidation step 2: trans-delta-2-enoyl-CoA, with 'plus H2O, minus H2O' over a double arrow, catalyzed by enoyl-CoA hydratase, gives L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA.
Beta-oxidation step 3: L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA with NAD plus giving NADH plus H plus over the arrow, catalyzed by hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, gives 3-ketoacyl-CoA.
Beta-oxidation step 4: 3-ketoacyl-CoA plus CoA-SH, catalyzed by thiolase, gives a shortened acyl-CoA plus acetyl-CoA.

Beta-oxidation of stearic acid shown as a grid of colored panels: the activation step to stearoyl-CoA at the top (yellow), then eight successive cycles, each panel showing the four reactions (dehydrogenation, hydration, dehydrogenation, thiolysis) that remove one acetyl-CoA, until the final cycle leaves two acetyl-CoA; labeled 'beta-Oxidation of stearic acid'.

Body mass index chart with weight in kilograms (bottom) and pounds (top) on the horizontal axis and height in meters and in feet and inches on the vertical axis; shaded bands mark underweight (BMI below 18.5, white), normal range (BMI 18.5 to 25, yellow), overweight (BMI 25 to 30, orange) and obese (BMI over 30, red).

Ketone body formation: two acetyl-CoA combine (thiolase) to acetoacetyl-CoA; HMG-CoA synthase adds a third acetyl-CoA to give beta-hydroxy-beta-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA); HMG-CoA lyase releases acetyl-CoA to give acetoacetate, which loses CO2 to give acetone or is reduced by NADH to D-beta-hydroxybutyrate; the three ketone bodies are highlighted in orange boxes.
Photograph of a bottle of urine test strips with a color chart on the label for reading ketone and other results.

Diagram of blood sugar regulation: when blood sugar is high, the pancreas releases insulin, which promotes glycogen synthesis in the liver and glucose uptake by tissue cells, lowering blood sugar; when blood sugar is low, the pancreas releases glucagon, which promotes glycogen breakdown to glucose in the liver, raising blood sugar.

Glycerol (three carbons each with an OH) plus ATP, with 'Glycerol kinase' over the arrow (Mg 2 plus, ADP released), gives glycerol-3-phosphate (a phosphate on one end carbon); then NAD plus with 'Glycerol phosphate dehydrogenase' (Zn 2 plus, NADH plus H plus released) gives dihydroxyacetone phosphate, with the middle carbon now a C=O.
597210: Processing of amino-acid nitrogen: alanine transfers its amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate (alanine aminotransferase, 1) giving pyruvate and L-glutamate; glutamate dehydrogenase (2) releases NH4 plus (which enters the urea cycle, circled in red) and regenerates alpha-ketoglutarate; glutamate-oxaloacetate transaminase (3) makes aspartate; glutamine synthetase (4) adds NH4 plus to glutamate to make glutamine, and glutaminase (5) releases it again.
NH4 plus plus bicarbonate (HCO3 minus) plus 2 ATP, with an arrow, gives carbamoyl phosphate (H2N-C(=O)-O-PO3 2 minus) plus 2 ADP plus Pi.

The urea cycle drawn across the mitochondrial matrix and cytoplasm: in the matrix, CPS-1 makes carbamoyl phosphate from NH3, CO2 and 2 ATP, and OTC joins it to ornithine to make citrulline; in the cytoplasm, ASS joins citrulline with aspartate (using ATP) to make argininosuccinate, ASL splits off fumarate to give arginine, and ARG1 hydrolyzes arginine to urea and ornithine, which re-enters the mitochondrion.
Structure of L-aspartate: HOOC-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH, drawn with a wedge bond to the NH2.

Where amino acid carbon skeletons enter metabolism, drawn around the citric acid cycle with a color legend (glucogenic in purple, ketogenic in green, both in red): alanine, glycine, threonine, cysteine, serine and tryptophan enter as pyruvate; tryptophan, tyrosine, phenylalanine, threonine, isoleucine, lysine and leucine as acetyl-CoA; arginine, proline, histidine and glutamine via glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate; threonine, methionine, isoleucine and valine as succinyl-CoA; tyrosine, phenylalanine and aspartate as fumarate; aspartate and asparagine as oxaloacetate, which leads through phosphoenolpyruvate to glucose.
597211: Lipoprotein classes plotted as circles of increasing size against particle diameter (5 to 800 nm, horizontal) and density (1.20 down to 0.95 g/mL, vertical): HDL (smallest, 50 percent lipid, 50 percent protein, density 1.063 to 1.21), LDL (80 percent lipid), IDL (85 percent), VLDL (92 percent) and chylomicrons (largest, 99 percent lipid, 1 percent protein, density below 0.95).
597213: Ketone body formation: two molecules of acetyl-CoA combine to acetoacetyl-CoA (releasing CoASH); a third acetyl-CoA adds to give beta-hydroxy-beta-methylglutaryl-CoA, which loses acetyl-CoA to give acetoacetate; acetoacetate is reduced by NADH to beta-hydroxybutyrate or loses CO2 to give acetone; the three ketone bodies are bracketed at the bottom.
597215: The principal events and sites of protein digestion: in the mouth nothing happens; in the stomach HCl and pepsin denature and partially hydrolyze proteins; in the small intestine trypsin, chymotrypsin, aminopeptidase and carboxypeptidase give small peptides and amino acids, which are absorbed by active transport through the intestinal lining into the blood.

Activation of pancreatic enzymes: enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen to trypsin; trypsin then converts more trypsinogen to trypsin and converts chymotrypsinogen to chymotrypsin (dashed arrows show the activations).

A short peptide drawn out with the peptide bonds that each enzyme cleaves marked in red: aminopeptidase at the N-terminal bond, pepsin next to aromatic residues, chymotrypsin or pepsin next to phenylalanine, trypsin next to lysine, and carboxypeptidase at the C-terminal bond.
